SpaceX targets first Starship orbital test on September 22

Reuters
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:52 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Sept 15 (Reuters) - SpaceX said on Tuesday it was preparing to launch its next ‌Starship flight test as soon as ‌September 22, a mission expected to send the vehicle ​into orbit for the first time and deploy Starlink V3 satellites.

Starship's 14th test flight would mark a major leap in the rocket's development ‌over its last ⁠test in July, which flew a suborbital trajectory that took the spacecraft ⁠into space before returning it to Earth without completing an orbit.

The company plans to place ​Starship into ​orbit around Earth, ​a milestone that would ‌allow it to test the vehicle over a longer-duration flight and deploy the first batch of Starlink V3 satellites.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The mission, pending regulatory approval, is expected to last nearly 10 hours, ‌with Starship flying about ​275 km above Earth and ​completing about ​six orbits before splashing down in ‌the Pacific Ocean west of ​Chile.

SpaceX plans ​to test the booster's launch, separation, boostback and splashdown procedures, advancing the company toward ​its goal ‌of a fully reusable orbital launch system.

(Reporting ​by Harshita Mary Varghese in Bengaluru; ​Editing by Tasim Zahid)

data.title: Judge Accuses Trump Of 'Linguistic Gymnastics' To Get His Name On Kennedy Center
data.description:
Judge Accuses Trump Of 'Linguistic Gymnastics' To Get His Name On Kennedy Center

Sara Boboltz
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:47 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A federal judge on Tuesday smacked down the latest efforts to plaster President Donald Trump's name on the Kennedy Center, stating that adding it would violate an earlier court ruling and the will of Congress.

Judge Christopher R. Cooper accused the president and his allies of "linguistic gymnastics" and "play[ing] word games" and in clear defiance of "common sense."

Politics: Trump Loses It After Judge Rules He Can't Slap His Name On Kennedy Center

He also suggested that, while Trump's allies argued in court filings that adding Trump's name was necessary to prevent the center from falling into ruin, the opposite appeared to be true in practice, as artists pulled out of performances in protest of the president's stunt.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Cooper said that the Kennedy Center board, which Trump packed with loyalists, cannot install Trump's name on the front facade, nor can they christen the grounds of the performing arts venue "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

The board voted last month to add to the building, right below "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts," the words "restored and renovated by" in small font and, below that, in font matching the size of Kennedy's name, "President Donald J. Trump."

Cooper sided Tuesday with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), who brought the suit last year in opposition to Trump's changes.

Politics: Court Says Trump Can't Name The Kennedy Center After Himself

He argued that Trump's allies were bending over backwards to avoid characterizing the additions as a type of "memorial," using instead words like "recognition," "plaque," "testimonial" and "acknowledgment," seeing as the Center's governing statute says no additional memorials can be installed there.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"But common sense dictates that the words 'renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump' establish a memorial. Defendants themselves define a 'memorial' as 'anything meant to help people remember some person or event, as a statute, holiday, etc.,'" the judge said.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Later, he wrote that "[l]inguistic gymnastics cannot extricate the Kennedy Center's Board from an operative judicial order or the governing statute it was designed to enforce."

A federal performing arts venue was established by Congress in 1958, and renamed in honor of President John F. Kennedy, a great supporter of the arts, in the wake of his 1963 assassination.

Politics: Trump Loses It After Key Republican Reportedly Backs Dem For 1st Time In 30 Years

"Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," Cooper wrote.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

If a particular fundraising goal is met in the future, the center's board also planned to add another couple of lines to the front facade: "endowed by" in small font and then "The Trump Kennedy Center Fund" in larger font. Cooper said that it was premature of him to address that line before the $100 million goal was met.

The center's facade has been partially covered for months as the lawsuit about Trump's name played out in the courts.

data.title: Trump lashes out at Supreme Court justices after ballots ruling
data.description:
Trump lashes out at Supreme Court justices after ballots ruling

Reuters
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:50 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media after traveling to Ireland

1 of 2
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media aboard Air Force One, en route to Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, U.S., following a two-day visit to Ireland, September 13, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump lashed out on Tuesday at his own Supreme Court appointees a day after the top U.S. judicial body declined to allow a U.S. Postal Service rule restricting the use of mail-in ballots in the November midterm elections ‌in his latest acidic criticism of the court after an unfavorable ruling.

"This Supreme Court is bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left into ‌making decisions that have set America back at least a hundred years," Trump wrote on social media.

"These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they ​are merely a shell of their original selves," Trump continued on Truth Social, without naming any of the justices. "It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country's history."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump appointed three justices — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — during his first term as president, building a 6-3 conservative majority and allowing the court to steer a dramatic rightward course since 2020.

On Monday, the court's decision preventing implementation of the ‌rule, which the Postal Service adopted at the president's ⁠direction, was brief and unsigned, as is typical when it handles emergency requests. Trump called it a "horrible, highly political, ruling."

Only conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas publicly dissented. Trump referred to them as "legends, both."

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters ⁠later that the Trump administration would comply with the court's decision.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It was not the first time Trump directed harsh words at his own appointees. After the court in February struck down his sweeping global tariffs that it found he had imposed illegally using a law meant for national emergencies, Trump reserved special ire for Gorsuch and Barrett, who ​were ​in the majority in that 6-3 ruling.

"I think it's an embarrassment to their families, you ​wanna know the truth, the two of them," Trump said ‌from a White House lectern.

In Tuesday's post, Trump revived his grievances about the tariffs ruling and a separate ruling in June against his attempt to restrict birthright citizenship.

THE BALLOTS RULE

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The USPS regulation would have required states to provide voter-specific data and use agency-approved mail-ballot envelopes that would be tracked using barcodes. The Postal Service could then refuse to send out ballots that do not comply with the new standards or are associated with voters who do not appear on the lists.

Critics warned that the measure could disrupt the delivery of thousands of legitimate ballots as the November 3 vote approaches and cause chaos given imminent plans by ‌many states to send out mail ballots to eligible voters.

The administration said the new rule ​would prevent voter fraud, though evidence of such fraud is rare.

Trump's fellow Republicans are locked ​in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. ​Restricting mail-in ballots would stand to benefit Republicans given that Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according to various surveys.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump signed ‌his executive order targeting mail-in ballots in March after years ​of casting doubt on their security, though ​he often votes by mail himself. Trump has made false claims of widespread fraud in U.S. elections including his 2020 loss to former Democratic President Joe Biden.

"It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself," Trump wrote on Tuesday of the mail ballot ruling.

The Supreme Court has ​delivered several election-related rulings in recent months that have ‌benefited Republicans, although last Thursday it blocked Missouri from using a redrawn congressional map that favors Republicans. That was a setback to Trump ​and his party's chances of maintaining its slim majority in the U.S. House of Representatives in November's elections.

(Reporting by Bhargav Acharya, Doina ​Chiacu and Andrew Chung; Editing by Susan Heavey, Caitlin Webber and Will Dunham)

data.title: Kennedy Center board votes to close for renovations after judge blocks Trump's name from facade
data.description:
Kennedy Center board votes to close for renovations after judge blocks Trump's name from facade

By Bo Erickson and Mike Scarcella
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:48 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Bo Erickson and Mike Scarcella

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The board of the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts voted on Tuesday to shut down the center for repairs, a source familiar with the matter said, shortly after a federal judge ‌blocked the center from adding President Donald Trump's name to the building facade for a second time.

The center's board of trustees, which is ‌made up of Trump appointees with Trump himself serving as chairman, has said the iconic performing arts center is in dire need of immediate repairs and approved a plan backed by the ​president as part of his expansive campaign to remake America's capital city.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In a social media post on Tuesday, Trump shared video of what was described as corrosion and deterioration around the building.

"We have already wasted more than 6 months 'playing around' in Court," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

Earlier in the day, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington issued an order temporarily halting the center's latest proposal to put Trump's name on the memorial to Kennedy, the U.S. president who was assassinated ‌in 1963.

In addition, Cooper said the center's board cannot ⁠proceed with plans to rename the campus where it sits the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress' blessing," Cooper wrote.

The board has argued ⁠that adding Trump's name in honor of his efforts was necessary to ensure his continued commitment to its survival.

"The Board understands that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the Center," the board wrote in a draft ​resolution ​ahead of the meeting.

Trump's campaign to remake the center is part of his broader ​effort to leave his cultural and aesthetic mark on the ‌U.S. capital, including a large new ballroom to replace the White House East Wing he ordered demolished, a troubled renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and a planned "triumphal arch" near the nation's main cemetery honoring its war dead.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Tuesday's ruling came in a lawsuit filed by Democratic U.S. Representative Joyce Beatty, who serves on the center's board by virtue of her position in Congress. Trump has told the center's lawyers he plans to appeal the ruling, the source familiar with the matter said.

SECOND RULING FROM JUDGE

Cooper had previously ordered the center in May to remove Trump's name from the building after the center changed its marble ‌facade in December to read "The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for ​the Performing Arts." At that time, Cooper also blocked the center from closing down, finding that ​the board had not adequately considered the consequences.

Workers stripped Trump's name ​from the center in June and left the exterior masked by scaffolding and a white tarpaulin.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In a vote on August ‌13, the board signed off on the addition of an inscription ​honoring Trump and renaming the center's plaza ​after Trump.

The 10 options for how the president's inscription could be rendered included: "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" and "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump."

The draft resolution also said the center's finances are dire, and it will be unable to ​honor its payroll obligations or routine maintenance contracts "within a ‌matter of weeks."

After Trump began exerting more direct control over the Kennedy Center last year, artists canceled performances in protest, the Washington ​National Opera and the National Symphony Orchestra were forced to find other venues, and revenue cratered.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson and Mike Scarcella ​in Washington; Writing by Joseph Ax; editing by Scott Malone and Aurora Ellis)

data.title: Sanders and Bannon call for AI limits as public unease grows
data.description:
Sanders and Bannon call for AI limits as public unease grows

By Courtney Rozen
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:29 pm UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

"March on Washington 2026: Defend the Vote" rally and march for voting rights in Washington

1 of 2
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders (I–VT) speaks during the "March on Washington 2026: Defend the Vote" rally and march for voting rights in Washington, D.C., U.S., August 28, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

By Courtney Rozen

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Progressive U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a close ally of President Donald Trump, called on Tuesday for restrictions on AI systems, uniting two political adversaries around concerns that the technology will harm humans.

The two appeared at the same Washington gathering and warned of the potentially catastrophic consequences AI poses to humanity, as concern about its ‌risks spreads beyond Washington and Silicon Valley.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Speaking first, Sanders, a self-described democratic socialist, warned about the "growing threat" of AI and said the industry needed to be regulated with binding safety rules.

"AI has the ‌potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs, wiping out entire professions and making it harder for our young people to enter the workforce."

He added, "As many scientists believe could happen, this technology will escape human control with potentially catastrophic consequences."

Sanders drew applause from the room when he ​criticized tech executives for centralizing control over AI technology, including SpaceX CEO and former Trump adviser Elon Musk.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Last month, we learned that AI has been used for the first time ever to create new viruses. In the wrong hands, this could lead to new bioweapons and a potential global pandemic that could lead to the deaths of tens of millions of people," Sanders said.

Sanders called on Trump to negotiate a treaty with Chinese President Xi Jinping at their summit next week to pause AI development.

Bannon, a former White House strategist during Trump's first presidential term, has criticized Trump's approach to overseeing AI, placing the blame for the president's unwillingness to regulate the technology squarely on tech companies. On his Monday podcast, ‌Bannon said Congress should not pass laws that prohibit states from enforcing their ⁠own rules for the technology.

On Tuesday, Bannon called AI the defining issue of our time.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Here's what we have to do first: to slow down the pace so that we can understand exactly what's going on," Bannon said. He praised Sanders for the way he summarized the risks of AI and said the country has to rise above partisanship on ⁠the issue.

"I don't think you could find any too harder partisans than Bernie Sanders on the left and Steve Bannon on the right," he said.

Bannon said Congress will take too long to pass legislation slowing the development of AI. "This is going to have to be executive action," Bannon said.

He said the U.S. must cut off China from American-made computer chips.

UNLIKELY BEDFELLOWS

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The decision of Sanders and Bannon, who are on opposite ends of America's ideological divide, to speak at the same gathering on Tuesday underscores ​how ​concerns over AI and data centers are cutting across party lines and producing unlikely political bedfellows.

Trump on Monday downplayed concerns expressed by industry ​leaders over the weekend about the misuse of artificial intelligence harming people, saying the ‌U.S. already has guardrails in place for the powerful technology.

Backing Trump's position on Tuesday, Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson said there cannot be a moratorium on artificial intelligence development without losing the competitive edge to China and that AI companies can regulate themselves.

"They can self-regulate. They don't need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow it down, they should," Johnson told reporters.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The view that regulations will harm U.S. companies' ability to compete with their Chinese counterparts is shared by tech executives, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Recent surveys have found majorities of Americans worry the technology could be used to eliminate jobs, raise costs for families or otherwise cause social harm.

BACK FROM RECESS

The U.S. House of Representatives ended its long summer break on Monday, with members in the House and Senate holding private conversations about whether or not to legislate on AI, especially after Trump said there ‌was no need for legislative action.

Congress has been criticized in the past for lacking the collective expertise to rein in or ​regulate technology companies.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Speaking to Reuters, Republican Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio said, "This process of legislating takes so long. Imagine AI four years in. ​We're dealing with stuff that isn't even relevant in four years."

Residents in several states have also challenged ​proposals for new data centers, a critical component of the AI boom. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published in June, 77% of Americans worry AI-driven data centers will raise electricity costs.

Anthropic ‌researcher Jacob Coxon captured public attention last week when he said he resigned from ​the company, in part because the "people building AI earnestly believe ​that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

Also on Tuesday, Andrew Ferguson, the chairman of the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, expressed suspicions over AI companies seeking antitrust exemptions while they also lobby for new regulations.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Reuters previously reported that U.S. senators are debating a bill that would block states from enforcing their own laws governing certain risks posed by AI models. Previously, efforts to restrict state ​AI laws failed in the U.S. Senate.

Sanders and Bannon addressed the same event ‌as AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler, who leads the largest federation of labor unions in the U.S.

Sanders, along with House progressive Rep. Greg Casar, has called for the U.S. to pass legislation halting ​development of AI tools that are capable of "overthrowing or undermining the U.S. government," until the government creates a new agency to police the technology. Casar and Sanders have not released specifics.

(Reporting by ​Courtney Rozen. Additional reporting by Tim Reid, Alexandra Alper and Richard Cowan. Editing by David Gregorio and Nick Zieminski)

data.title: Texas Republican's post on Asian Americans at UT Austin sparks accusations of racism
data.description:
Texas Republican's post on Asian Americans at UT Austin sparks accusations of racism

By David Hood-Nuño
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:21 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By David Hood-Nuño

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - A Republican nominee for a Texas office drew bipartisan criticism after posting a photo from a University of Texas football game that critics called racist, portraying the Austin campus as dominated by foreign students contrary to enrollment data.

Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, drew a ‌sharp rebuke from fellow Republicans as well as Democrats after posting a crowd shot at a University of Texas football game, while suggesting that what appeared to be ‌students of South Asian descent reflected a large foreign-born or international student presence on campus.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," French posted ​to his X account. He went on to claim that UT prioritizes foreign students in admissions and feared Texans were losing opportunities at the university.

"I weep for the families in Texas who can't get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans," he said.

But enrollment figures released by the University of Texas at Austin show international students account for less than 10% of the total student body. Total enrollment reached 55,000 students for the fall 2025 semester, including 5,140 international students. Texas residents make up 80.5% of all enrolled students.

For the undergraduate class, international students make up 4.3%, and a state law requires ‌90% of every incoming freshman class to be Texas residents. UT ⁠Austin automatically admits the top 5% of performers — who are also Texas residents — at every high school in the state.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Texas legislature designed the initiative to promote diversity without explicitly considering race. As in most of the country, Texas high school students are separated by geography, income and demographics, and ⁠by guaranteeing admission to top students at each high school, the statewide policy helps ensure universities draw from a broad cross-section of Texas communities.

That means more than 90% of students at UT Austin are domestic, and more than four out of every five are Texans.

Vedant Nair, 24, who graduated from UT in 2024, said his parents immigrated to Oklahoma in the 1990s from Mumbai so his father could pursue an MBA ​at ​Oklahoma State University. Nair was born in Oklahoma City and recalls running around in a child-size OSU Cowboys ​football helmet and driving a mini John Deere tractor. His upbringing, he ‌said, was no different than those of his fellow Texans after his family moved to Dallas in elementary school.

Attending UT Austin was a dream come true, and a normal, American experience, he said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"If you stripped away my name and skin color, I think my story is pretty similar to a lot of other Texans at massive public high schools," Nair said. "The point is that myself, and all the other kids in that picture, are just regular American kids."

University spokespeople and French did not respond to a request for comment.

The debate touches on a broader political argument that non-U.S. citizens are "displacing" American students at elite public universities, and the country at large.

French's remarks drew criticism from political figures and other social media users, who characterized the posts as racist or xenophobic.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Rodney ‌Coates, a sociology professor at Miami University in Ohio, said French's comments echoed longstanding anti-immigrant and anti-Asian narratives ​in the U.S. that have historically portrayed minority groups as threats to opportunities for others.

"It's easier to come up ​with a racist argument to organize a group of people under the presumption that, ​hey, they're hurting your chances," Coates said. Such appeals often have little to do with the people being targeted and instead seek to mobilize voters ‌by portraying them as victims. "Hate is one of the easiest means of ​organizing," he said.

University figures show white students made up ​about 31.5% of enrollment in 2024 to 2025, Hispanic students 25.5% and Asian students 22.4%.

University reporting treats race and ethnicity separately from international student status, meaning most students categorized as Asian are U.S. citizens or permanent residents rather than international students.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The image French shared was a screenshot from a video posted by the official athletics account at UT Austin. He did ​not include information identifying the citizenship, immigration status, residency or enrollment ‌status of any individuals shown.

For Nair, the unfortunate part of French's post was that it criticized a high point in school-pride history: the football team defeated The ​Ohio State University, the No. 1-ranked football team in the country.

"I don't think there is anything more American than people in cowboy hats yelling their heads off ​after one of the greatest comeback wins in college football history," he said.

(Reporting by David Hood-Nuño)

data.title: FBI's Patel defends change in 'bestiality' hiring practice as lawmakers seek answers
data.description:
FBI's Patel defends change in 'bestiality' hiring practice as lawmakers seek answers

By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:31 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, in Washington

1 of 2
FBI Director Kash Patel testifies before a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - FBI Director Kash Patel told lawmakers on Tuesday he changed the bureau's hiring standards to eliminate bestiality as an automatic disqualifier because he did not want to bar trafficking victims who had been forced to have sex with animals, drawing ‌an incredulous response from Republicans and Democrats alike.

"We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked," Patel said in response ‌to one question during his testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Patel later said that previous regulations disqualified "any individual who participated on either side of it."

"Either side of what, the bestiality?" Senator John ​Kennedy, a Republican, asked. "So you disqualified the animal?"

"We have great canines, but we're not going to disqualify them," Patel said, laughing.

In a more than four-hour oversight hearing, his first appearance before the Senate since May, Patel also faced questions about his agency's handling of files related to the late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, the use of taxpayer funds for personal travel and allegations that he has politicized the FBI.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But it was his revised hiring standards that drew some of the most noteworthy questions.

"Why would ‌you even get into bestiality?" Kennedy asked, after noting that ⁠prospective FBI agents may be wondering if their political point of view matters. Patel said he was told that some trafficking victims forced into bestiality had been previously disqualified from jobs.

"But you're not telling us today that if a human being had ⁠sex with an animal, they can still be an FBI agent?" Kennedy asked. Patel said no.

Republicans asked Patel about the FBI's probes into a prior federal investigation of Republican President Donald Trump's attempts to overturn his loss to Democrat Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election, an issue Republican committee chair Senator Chuck Grassley has called a top priority for the ​panel.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Tuesday's ​appearance came after prosecutor Joe DiGenova, who had been leading a Justice Department investigation that sought ​to show that Trump was the victim of a criminal conspiracy, ‌abruptly resigned last week.

FBI AND ELECTIONS

Patel appeared to confirm media reports that a dozen FBI Iran experts were fired this year because of their alleged "weaponization" efforts, namely that they were part of the investigation into Trump's alleged retention of classified documents.

"I think what's most important is to not have a weaponized FBI," Patel said. "I will endeavor every single day to make sure we have no one there that is doing that."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Patel, a Trump appointee, has been a subject of controversy since he took over as head of the FBI. He drew criticism over media reports about him scuba diving at a Pearl Harbor memorial, and for drinking beer while celebrating ‌with the gold-medal-winning U.S. men's hockey team at the Milan Winter Olympics.

He has also faced scrutiny ​over his use of a government plane and luxury cars, and Trump administration investigations into journalists ​and their sources.

Patel said in a letter released ahead of the hearing ​that he has reimbursed personal travel expenses and said the luxury cars were cheaper than others the FBI has previously bought.

Patel ‌grew increasingly frustrated with Democrats who questioned him over his personal ​conduct, including asking Senator Peter Welch if ​he was hard of hearing.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Everyone sees you for the complete and total fraud you are," Patel told Welch, who was asking whether FBI resources had been used to investigate an Atlantic magazine journalist who had written about Patel's alleged excessive drinking.

Patel also said the FBI would monitor the midterm ​elections from its field offices but told Senator Amy Klobuchar, a ‌Minnesota Democrat, he would follow the law that bars agents from being deployed inside polling places on Election Day.

But Patel later refused to pledge ​that he would not interfere in the election.

"I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies," Patel said.

(Reporting ​by Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff; Editing by Andy Sullivan, Will Dunham, Bill Berkrot and Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: US agency orders Tesla to answer questions on Cybercab certification
data.description:
US agency orders Tesla to answer questions on Cybercab certification

Reuters
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:24 pm UTC
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

data.description:
Harry Enten Spots 1 Key Voting Bloc Saying 'Adios' To Trump

Marco Margaritoff
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:24 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten said President Donald Trump has lost a colossal amount of approval from one key voting bloc that helped reelect him in 2024, citing recent polls on Tuesday confirming that prior support from the group has plainly said, "Adios, amigos."

"Oh, my goodness gracious," said Enten during a "News Central" appearance. "Oy oy oy, no bueno if you're the president of the United States, because just take a look here: He had a massive breakthrough in 2024; he won working-class Latinos!"

Politics: Harry Enten Says 1 Key Group Has Sharply Flipped On Donald Trump

Enten cited Pew Research Center data and CNN-SSRS polls from 2026 suggesting Trump, who won the demographic in the 2024 election against former Vice President Kamala Harris, has landed the GOP in major trouble ahead of the upcoming midterms in November.

"He won non-college Latino voters by a point over Kamala Harris," said Enten. "That's a major breakthrough for a Republican president, or a Republican running for president. But that win that he had? Adios, amigos. Goodbye, see you later."

He continued, "Look at his net approval rating now in an average of polls, CNN-SSRS polls across 2026: He's 42 points underwater. That is a switcheroo ... shifting away from the president of the United States, his support rapidly declining, plummeting among working-class Latinos ― a group that helped get him elected back in 2024."

Although Trump won the 2024 election on vows to boost the economy and promises to revive U.S. manufacturing ― and instead launched mass deportations and deadly immigration raids shortly after returning to office — he appears to have lost major support from Latinos since then.

Politics: Harry Enten Spots The 'Bonkers' Way This Group Is Turning On Trump

"There has been a massive, massive backlash," Enten noted Tuesday.

The data guru explained that non-college Latinos helped Trump beat Harris on the issue of immigration by 9 points in the 2024 election, citing an average of CNN-SSRS polls, but now has a net approval rating of -47 points on the issue from that same demographic.

"You don't see shifts away from a president of the United States of 56 points unless you have done something absolutely terribly wrong in the minds of the voters," said Enten. "These are terrible, terrible numbers."

Trump recently hit the worst approval rating of his presidency amid a nationwide affordability crisis that he has repeatedly dismissed and a costly war on Iran that he himself started. Enten noted the resulting backlash from voters should have Republicans "running scared."
